stories.head: Russia and Ukraine agree large prisoner swap after Abu Dhabi talks
stories.say: Russia and Ukraine have agreed a large exchange of prisoners of war after two days of American-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi, though neither side has given ground on territory.
stories.stand: Both delegation leaders confirmed the exchange, but its size was not given and the two sides remain far apart on land.
body: Russia and Ukraine agreed a large exchange of prisoners of war after two days of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi, ABC News reported, citing AP, Reuters and AFP. The size of the swap was not given.

Russia's lead negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, and Ukraine's, Rustem Umerov, both confirmed it. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who did not attend, called the second day constructive and quite substantive. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the meeting very productive but said a breakthrough would take time.

Territory remains the main sticking point, Euronews reported: Moscow demands all of Donbas and Kyiv refuses to cede land. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov rejected a ceasefire. US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are due to meet Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

stories.head: Russia's ambassador to the US, Alexander Darchiev, dies at 66
stories.say: Russia's ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, has died suddenly at sixty-six, the Russian foreign ministry said on Wednesday. No cause was given.
stories.stand: The veteran diplomat had held the Washington post since early 2025 after serving as ambassador to Canada.
body: Alexander Darchiev, Russia's ambassador to the United States, died suddenly on Wednesday aged 66, Russia's foreign ministry said. It gave no cause of death, Al Jazeera and Euronews reported.
He took up the post in early 2025, replacing Anatoly Antonov. He had been ambassador to Canada from 2014 to 2021 and earlier served at the Russian embassy in Washington.
The ministry described him as an outstanding diplomat and a kind colleague. Euronews noted he had called Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine a necessary measure.

stories.head: Iran says the ball is in Washington's court on a deal
stories.say: Iran's chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, says Tehran has sent its conditions for ending the war to Washington, and the Strait of Hormuz will never return to its pre-war status.
stories.stand: Tehran's chief negotiator set out conditions including an end to the US naval blockade, as another official ruled out sending enriched uranium abroad.
body: Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's parliament speaker and chief negotiator, told Al Jazeera that Tehran had sent its conditions to Washington through a Qatari mediator and was awaiting an official reply.

The conditions include lifting the US naval blockade and sanctions, releasing frozen funds and an explicit announcement that the war is over. He said the Strait of Hormuz would never return to its pre-war status and that Iran and Oman had agreed to oversee it jointly.

Separately, CBS News reported that Mohsen Rezaei, of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said Tehran would not let enriched nuclear material leave the country. The US wants Iran to give up its highly enriched uranium.

The insurer Allianz Trade estimated war damage to Gulf states at more than $200 billion, according to CBS News.

stories.head: At least nine killed in Israeli strikes across Gaza
stories.say: Israeli attacks killed at least nine Palestinians across Gaza, including four at the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, according to Gaza's civil defence.
stories.stand: The deaths came as the UN appealed for waterproof tents for families affected by flooding.
body: Israeli attacks killed at least nine Palestinians across Gaza, Al Jazeera reported. At least four were killed at the Nasser Medical Complex in western Khan Younis, according to Gaza Civil Defence spokesperson Mahmoud Basal.
Two people were killed in a strike on a displaced family's tent in Sheikh Radwan, in northern Gaza City, and three men were killed in separate attacks elsewhere.

Gaza's Government Media Office said at least 70,000 tents had flooded. UNICEF says 106,000 people were directly affected. The UN has appealed for waterproof tents. Al Jazeera's report did not include an Israeli military response.

stories.head: More than a million people in Lebanon face acute food shortages
stories.say: More than a million people in Lebanon, nearly a quarter of the population, face acute food shortages, United Nations agencies said on Wednesday, after two wars in under two years.
stories.stand: The FAO, the World Food Programme and Lebanon's agriculture ministry expect the figure to reach 1.15 million by mid-2027.
body: More than one million people in Lebanon, nearly a quarter of the population, face acute food shortages, according to a joint statement from the FAO, the World Food Programme and Lebanon's agriculture ministry, Al Jazeera reported.
The agencies expect the figure to reach 1.15 million by mid-2027. They blame two conflicts in under two years, scarce jobs, high debt and rising food and fuel costs.
Lebanese authorities estimate the two Israel-Hezbollah wars since October 2023 cost about $27bn. About 300,000 people remain displaced.

stories.head: Storm Charles shuts every school in Portugal
stories.say: Portugal shut all its schools and non-essential public services on Wednesday as Storm Charles arrived, and more than three hundred flights were cancelled.
stories.stand: About 8,000 schools shut, a first in living memory for a forecast storm, but no casualties were reported.
body: Portugal closed all of its roughly 8,000 schools and non-essential public services on Wednesday as Storm Charles arrived, Al Jazeera and Euronews reported. Civil servants were told to work from home.
More than 300 flights were cancelled. The weather agency IPMA recorded gusts above 120 km/h in some areas. Lisbon's Web Summit cancelled the day's events.
Prime Minister Luis Montenegro chaired a crisis unit. No casualties were reported, and Interior Minister Luis Neves rejected claims that the authorities had overreacted.

stories.head: Spain holds first general strike since 2012 over housing
stories.say: Unions say four million Spanish workers joined Wednesday's general strike over housing costs, the first since twenty twelve. Police made forty arrests by midday.
stories.stand: The UGT and CCOO unions led the walkout, sparked by the eviction and death of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid.
body: Unions said four million workers joined a general strike over Spain's housing crisis on Wednesday, the first since 2012, ABC News reported, citing Reuters. Madrid's metro said peak-hour use was down 42% on the previous week.
Police reported 40 arrests by midday in 476 incidents. Unions said police used tear gas and batons and that 20 protesters were hurt. Some protesters smashed shop fronts in Madrid and Barcelona.

The strike was led by the UGT and CCOO unions and tenants' groups. It followed the eviction and later death of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called a snap election for 29 November.

stories.stand: Organisers had expected a record turnout, including foreign nationalist groups; no official crowd figure was given.

stories.head: Trinidad and Tobago's top court ends ban on gay sex
stories.say: Trinidad and Tobago's final court of appeal, the Privy Council in London, has ruled unanimously that a 1986 law cannot be used to prosecute consensual same-sex relations between adults.
stories.stand: The ruling ends a decade-long challenge led by activist Jason Jones; the UN human rights chief called it a milestone.
body: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, Trinidad and Tobago's final court of appeal, ruled unanimously on Tuesday that the 1986 Sexual Offences Act cannot be used to prosecute private, consensual same-sex relations between adults, Euronews reported.
The law had set prison terms of up to five years. The case was a decade-long challenge led by activists including Jason Jones.
The court said constitutional rights must remain practical and effective in the present day. UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the ruling a significant milestone.

stories.head: Congo military court sentences 66 soldiers to death
stories.say: A military court in eastern Congo has sentenced sixty-six soldiers to death for cowardice and mutiny after they allegedly fled fighting with rebels.
stories.stand: The verdict in Walikale, North Kivu, followed a 12-day trial; four soldiers were acquitted.
body: A military court in Walikale, in eastern Congo's North Kivu province, sentenced 66 soldiers to death after a 12-day trial, CBS News reported. Four were acquitted and one was jailed for 10 years.
The charges included cowardice, disobeying orders, mutiny and wasting ammunition, after the soldiers allegedly fled fighting with rebels. They were detained on 20 October.
Congo reinstated the death penalty in March 2024. Amnesty International said the decision would endanger the lives of hundreds of people.

stories.say: DNA tests have linked a female grizzly and her three cubs to the deaths of a mother and her daughter near Bella Coola in British Columbia. All four bears have been put down.
stories.stand: Conservation officers said the attack likely involved rare predatory behaviour.
body: DNA tests conclusively linked a female grizzly bear and her three yearling cubs to the deaths of a 48-year-old woman and her 20-year-old daughter near Bella Coola, British Columbia, officials said on Tuesday, CBS News reported.
The British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said the attack likely involved predatory behaviour, which Inspector Jeff Tyre called very rare.
All four bears were killed. Officials said bears involved in fatal attacks cannot be relocated. ABC News also reported that the bears had been put down.

stories.head: Novaya Gazeta shuts its Moscow office
stories.say: Novaya Gazeta, Russia's last openly critical newspaper, has closed its Moscow office after it was evicted and its media registration was revoked. The Kremlin called it a normal process.
stories.stand: Founder and Nobel laureate Dmitry Muratov attended a final editorial meeting as staff took down portraits of murdered colleagues.
body: Novaya Gazeta, Russia's last openly critical newspaper, has closed its Moscow office and stopped operating, Euronews reported. It had been evicted, its donations system shut down, its websites blocked and its media registration revoked.

Editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov held a final editorial meeting, attended by founder and Nobel laureate Dmitry Muratov. Staff took down portraits of six murdered journalists, including Anna Politkovskaya.
More than 400,000 articles have been archived. Reporters Without Borders, Amnesty International and the UN human rights office condemned the closure. The Kremlin called it a normal process.

stories.say: A forty-one-year-old American soldier has been arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of helping Russian intelligence. The Kremlin says it had nothing to do with it.
stories.stand: Counter-terror police say the arrest is not linked to the alleged Iran-backed plot against RAF Fairford.
body: A 41-year-old US Army soldier was arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of offences under the National Security Act 2023, British and US authorities said on Tuesday. Police searched two addresses in Gloucestershire, CBS News reported.

The suspected offences relate to protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service. Counter Terrorism Policing's Vicki Evans said the allegations were serious and the investigation was ongoing. The suspect is being held at a London police station.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the allegations were of the utmost concern, Euronews reported. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia had nothing to do with the arrest. Police say the case is not linked to other counter-terrorism inquiries.

stories.say: American prosecutors have charged three men with supporting Iran's Revolutionary Guard, including an alleged plot against RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire.
stories.stand: An eight-count indictment accuses them of links to almost 20 attacks or attempted attacks in Europe and North America.
body: The US Justice Department unsealed an eight-count indictment on Tuesday against three men accused of supporting Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kataib Hezbollah, ITV News and CBS News reported.

They are Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, who is held in New York, and Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, who are not in custody. Prosecutors allege al-Saadi directed and paid associates in the UK to prepare an attack on RAF Fairford.

Three vans were stopped near the base in late September and petrol was seized, ITV reported. Seven people have been arrested and bailed in the UK. Iran has denied involvement. The charges are allegations and have not been proven.

stories.stand: The US Air Force said aircraft routinely rotate, while US European Command declined to discuss protective measures.

stories.say: David Walliams has denied allegations, made in a joint media investigation, that he pursued teenage girls and vulnerable young women. He says he has not broken the law.
stories.stand: Several women describe conduct going back to 2003; Walliams says he is not a predator but acknowledges behaving thoughtlessly.
body: A three-year joint investigation by ITV News and the Guardian reports allegations from several women that David Walliams pursued them for sexual purposes when they were teenagers or vulnerable young women. The allegations date back to 2003.

One woman says he contacted her when she was 15. Others describe conduct at Britain's Got Talent and at the publisher HarperCollins. Walliams denies all the allegations, including any criminal behaviour.

He said he was not a sexual predator and had not broken the law, but acknowledged he had behaved thoughtlessly in some past relationships. He had sought a High Court injunction to stop the investigation. HarperCollins ended its relationship with him in December 2025.

stories.say: A Florida judge has refused to throw out Donald Trump's ten-billion-dollar defamation claim against the BBC over a Panorama edit. The BBC says it is surprised.
stories.stand: Judge Jeffrey Kuntz found the defamation claim plausibly alleged but dismissed a separate Florida trade practices claim.
body: Judge Jeffrey Kuntz of the US District Court in southern Florida on Tuesday rejected the BBC's bid to dismiss Donald Trump's $10bn defamation claim, CBS News and Al Jazeera reported. He dismissed a separate claim under Florida's deceptive trade practices law.
The case concerns a Panorama documentary that spliced together two clips of Trump's speech of 6 January 2021. The judge said whether Trump can prove his claims was a matter for another day.

The BBC said it was surprised by the decision but respected the court's authority, and remained confident in its position. It apologised for the edit in November 2025 but says there is no basis for a defamation claim.

stories.head: Home Office taken to High Court over child abuse inquiry reforms
stories.say: A charity has taken the Home Office to the High Court, arguing it has failed to adopt the twenty main reforms from the child sexual abuse inquiry.
stories.stand: The charity says only seven recommendations have been carried out; the Home Office says they carry no legal force.
body: The Maggie Oliver Foundation is suing the Home Office in the High Court in London over its alleged failure to adopt all 20 main reforms recommended by the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse, ITV News reported. The hearing began on Tuesday.

It is Congo's deadliest Ebola outbreak and the second-largest on record, behind West Africa's 2014 to 2016 epidemic, ITV reported. The WHO has backed two candidate vaccines for trials.

stories.stand: The study is observational, so it cannot show that stopping the drugs caused the extra risk.
body: A study of more than 80,000 adults with type 2 diabetes in Italy found that stopping GLP-1 drugs was linked to roughly double the combined risk of non-fatal heart attack, non-fatal stroke or death, Euronews reported.

There were about 4 events per 100 people a year among those who stopped, against 2 among those who continued. The study, in The Lancet Regional Health Europe, mostly involved earlier-generation drugs.
The design is observational, so it cannot prove cause and effect. People who stopped may have been sicker, and the authors call for more research.

body: Cardiac arrest was mentioned about 11 times more often in US FDA adverse event reports involving caffeine or other stimulant products than in reports for other products, according to a preliminary analysis presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions, ScienceDaily reported.
The analysis covered 28,345 reports from 2017 to 2025, of which 854 involved stimulant products. Heart attacks were mentioned about 4.5 times more often.
The reports are voluntary and lack exposure data, so the figures do not measure actual risk. An outside expert, Gregory Marcus, said the study does not prove the products cause these events.

stories.say: Fossil fuel carbon emissions are projected to fall slightly this year, the Global Carbon Budget says, but total emissions will still rise because of fires in Southeast Asia.
stories.stand: Scientists say the drop is driven by shocks, not structural change, and the 1.5C budget could be used up in under four years.
body: Fossil fuel CO2 emissions are projected to fall 0.4% in 2026, according to the Global Carbon Budget, Euronews reported. Oil emissions drop 1.9% while coal rises 0.6%.

The study's leader, Pierre Friedlingstein of the University of Exeter, said a fall driven by geopolitical shocks was not a sustainable solution. About 150 billion tonnes remain in the budget for the 1.5C limit, less than four years at current rates.

stories.stand: Argentina is offering a reward of 20 million pesos; Italy convicted him in his absence of terrorism-related crimes.
body: Leonardo Bertulazzi, 74, a former member of Italy's far-left Red Brigades, escaped house arrest in Argentina on Tuesday by climbing down from a fifth-floor flat with a rope and harness, Al Jazeera reported.

Italian courts convicted him in his absence of terrorism-related crimes, with a combined sentence of 27 years. Argentina's Supreme Court approved his extradition last year.

stories.stand: The Logos runs until the end of the year, with a live performance with 30 singers on 21 November.
body: An installation called The Logos at Oulu Cathedral in Finland turns fast radio burst data into sound, Space.com reported. Each burst's signal is converted into shifting pitches played through 12 speakers.

The installation has played daily since April and runs until the end of the year. A live performance with 30 singers is planned for 21 November.

stories.stand: The study, in the European Heart Journal, did not test a treatment or a routine blood test.
body: Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology profiled nearly 3,000 blood proteins and compared them with genetic data and health records, ScienceDaily reported. The study is published in the European Heart Journal.

They found that triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and lipoprotein(a) shared protein patterns linked to inflammation and vessel-wall changes, and to later heart disease. LDL-linked proteins related mainly to cholesterol build-up.
The study did not test a treatment or validate a blood test for routine use, and further research is needed.

stories.head: 2026 ozone hole was the largest in a decade, NASA and NOAA say
stories.say: This year's Antarctic ozone hole peaked on the eighteenth of September at the largest size in a decade, NASA and NOAA say, but long-term recovery remains on track.
stories.stand: Scientists blame an unusually large polar vortex; the hole is expected to heal by the 2070s.
body: The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole reached about 10.5 million square miles on 18 September, the seventh largest in 48 years of monitoring, NOAA and NASA said, ABC7 News reported.
Scientists said an unusually large polar vortex was to blame, because weather systems that normally break it up were weak in August and September. In 2025 the hole was the fifth smallest since 1992.
Long-term recovery remains on track, with the hole expected to heal by the 2070s, the agencies said.
